title: Guests as Christ (ch. 53)
hookLine: let all guests be received as Christ

cards: A knock at the monastery gate, late, after supper. Dusty boots, a pack, a stranger nobody was expecting.
Inside, the monks are just settling into quiet after a long day, and an unplanned visitor at the wrong hour can make a whole house sigh. Saint Benedict's Rule doesn't pretend the knock is convenient.
But chapter fifty-three tells the monks exactly who is standing at the gate, and it isn't just a stranger.

teach.b: The chapter opens: let all guests who come be received as Christ. Benedict gives the reason in Christ's own words from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was a stranger, and you took me in."
So the guest isn't an interruption to the monks' life with God. Some readers put it this way: the guest is that life arriving in person. Then Benedict turns it into a ceremony.
The superior and the brothers go out to meet the guest with every mark of love. They pray together first, and only then exchange the kiss of peace.
They bow their heads, or even lie down on the ground, honoring Christ, who is received in the guest.

teach.h: PRAYER, A BOW, WATER, WASHED FEET.
teach.b: The abbot pours water over the guest's hands, and the abbot and the whole community wash the guest's feet. Then a line that's easy to read past.

teach.h: MOST CARE FOR THE POOR AND PILGRIMS.
teach.b: Benedict asks for the greatest care for the poor and for pilgrims, because in them, he says, Christ is received more. The rich, he notes dryly, get honored anyway; people are in awe of them.
The poor depend on the welcome. Benedict is practical, too.

teach.h: A GUEST KITCHEN, SO THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.
teach.b: The abbot and guests get their own kitchen, so guests turning up at odd hours, and he says guests never stop turning up, don't throw the brothers' day into chaos.

teach.h: I WAS A STRANGER, AND YOU TOOK ME IN.
teach.b: A sensible brother is put in charge of the guest house. Nobody has to choose between keeping the house running and opening the door. The door opens because the house is ordered.

how: Benedictine monasteries keep guesthouses and receive retreatants and visitors, and Catholics often point to chapter fifty-three and Matthew 25 when they talk about hospitality.

o: welcoming every guest as Christ himself
a feast held for visiting bishops and abbots
letting in only guests who are Christians

p: pours water over the guest's hands
so late guests don't upset the day

s: in the Rule, guests are an interruption to be kept to a minimum
Benedict says to receive every guest as Christ, with prayer, a bow, and washed feet.
Benedict asks for special care for the poor and pilgrims
because in them, he says, Christ is received more; the rich get honored anyway.
Benedict's monks greet guests with a kiss first and pray afterward
they pray together first, then exchange the kiss of peace.

games.q: you're the monk at the gate. two visitors arrive together: a rich landowner and a tired pilgrim with nothing. who does the Rule say needs the greatest care?
o: the landowner: he could help the monastery.
the pilgrim: in the poor, Christ is received more.
neither: treat them exactly the same in every way.
games.why: Benedict asks for the greatest care for the poor and pilgrims; the rich, he notes, are honored anyway, out of awe.

practice: Bring to mind the people who will cross your threshold today, not only guests: the coworker at your desk, the kid home from school, the cashier, the delivery driver.
Pick one, maybe someone easy to overlook, and picture looking up, turning toward them, and greeting them as the guest of honor. If you pray, ask to see Christ in them; if not, just see them.

wordCard.voice: Guests as Christ. Benedict's rule for the knock at the gate: every guest is welcomed as Christ himself, the poor and pilgrims most of all. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from the chapter's opening line: received as Christ.

carryVoice: Your line: received as Christ. The poor, Benedict says, depend on the welcome most. See you tomorrow.
